title: Organic Chemistry: Reactions and Mechanisms
description: The second-year organic toolkit: acidity, stereochemistry, alkene and carbonyl chemistry, enolates, aromatic substitution, coupling, rearrangements, synthesis planning and spectral interpretation.

entries.name: Acidity, pKa and predicting reactions
entries.tagline: A table of pKa values lets you predict whether an acid–base reaction will go.

sections.text: Look at the stability of the conjugate base. The more stable the base, the stronger the acid. The factors can be remembered as ARIO.
points: Atom: the negative charge is more stable on a more electronegative atom (across a period) and on a larger atom (down a group). H–I is a stronger acid than H–F, and thiols are stronger than alcohols.
Resonance: delocalization spreads out the charge. Carboxylate and phenoxide ions are stabilized, so carboxylic acids and phenols are much stronger acids than alcohols.
Inductive effect: nearby electron-withdrawing groups (F, Cl, C=O) stabilize the negative charge. Trifluoroacetic acid (pKa 0.5) is far stronger than acetic acid (4.76).
Orbital (hybridization): more s character holds the electrons closer to the nucleus. C–H acidity goes sp (25) > sp² (44) > sp³ (50).

equations: K = 10^(pKa of the acid on the left − pKa of the acid on the right)
sections.text: Equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid and the weaker base. Written as acid + base ⇌ conjugate base + conjugate acid, K = 10^(pKa(product acid) − pKa(reactant acid)). Example: ethoxide (conjugate acid, ethanol, pKa 16) removes a proton from a ketone α–H (pKa 20) only to a small extent (K = 10⁻⁴), so enolate forms only in small amounts. Sodium amide (conjugate acid pKa 38) deprotonates a terminal alkyne (pKa 25) completely.

quiz.q: Which is the stronger acid?
Which C–H bond is the most acidic?

entries.name: Conjugation and π molecular orbitals
entries.tagline: When p orbitals line up, the electrons spread out, which lowers the energy and changes the reactivity.

sections.text: A conjugated system has alternating single and multiple bonds, with overlapping p orbitals across several atoms. The π electrons are delocalized over all of them.
Hydrogenating 1,3-butadiene releases about 239 kJ/mol, but two isolated C=C bonds (twice 127 kJ/mol) would release about 254 kJ/mol. The conjugated diene is about 15 kJ/mol more stable.

points: Four p orbitals give four molecular orbitals, ψ₁ to ψ₄, with 0, 1, 2 and 3 nodes. The four π electrons fill ψ₁ and ψ₂.

ψ₂ is the HOMO and ψ₃ is the LUMO. The gap between them decreases as the conjugation grows, which is why longer conjugated molecules absorb at longer wavelength, and why β-carotene is orange. The same pattern comes from the particle in a box model.
The allyl cation, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺, is stabilized by resonance, so allylic and benzylic carbocations are much more stable than ordinary primary ones.

sections.text: HBr adds to butadiene to give two products. The 1,2-adduct forms faster, by attack at the carbocation carbon nearest the charge, and dominates at −80 °C (kinetic control). The 1,4-adduct has the more substituted double bond and is more stable, and dominates at 40 °C when the reaction can reverse (thermodynamic control). A low temperature and an irreversible reaction favor the kinetic product, and a high temperature and a reversible reaction favor the thermodynamic one.

quiz.q: At low temperature, which product of HBr addition to butadiene is favored?

entries.name: R/S and E/Z nomenclature and Fischer projections
entries.tagline: The rules that give every stereoisomer an unambiguous name.

points: Rank the four groups on a stereocenter by the atomic number of the atom attached to it. Higher atomic number is higher priority.
If there is a tie, move outward to the next atoms until a difference is found. Compare the sets of atoms, in order of priority.
A double or triple bond counts as if the atom were duplicated at the far end: C=O counts as C with (O, O).

sections.text: Point the lowest-priority group away from you. If the path from priority 1 to 2 to 3 is clockwise, the center is R (rectus). If counterclockwise, it is S (sinister). If the lowest-priority group is toward you, assign it and reverse the answer. For CHFClBr the order is Br > Cl > F > H.

For an alkene, rank the two groups on each carbon. If the higher-priority groups are on the same side, the alkene is Z (zusammen). If they are on opposite sides, it is E (entgegen). Z is not always the same as cis.

points: A Fischer projection shows a chain vertically with each stereocenter at a crossing. Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away.
Swapping two groups at a stereocenter inverts it. Turning the projection by 180° in the plane leaves it unchanged, but turning by 90° inverts all the centers.
In sugars, D means that the OH on the highest-numbered stereocenter is on the right.

quiz.q: In CIP rules, what is the highest priority group among Br, Cl, F, H?

entries.name: Stereochemical outcomes and asymmetric synthesis
entries.tagline: Predicting and controlling the three-dimensional result of a reaction.

facts: Different stereoisomers of the starting material give different stereoisomers of the product, because of the mechanism. SN2 inversion and E2 anti elimination are examples.
One stereoisomer is formed in preference to others, when more than one could form.

points: Syn (both groups on the same face): catalytic hydrogenation, hydroboration, osmium tetroxide dihydroxylation, epoxidation, cyclopropanation.
Anti (opposite faces): halogenation through a bromonium ion, halohydrin formation, oxymercuration, ring opening of epoxides.

sections.text: When a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl next to a stereocenter, the faces are different, so one diastereomer is favored. The Felkin–Anh model predicts it, with the nucleophile approaching past the smallest group and anti to the largest or most electron-withdrawing group.
Making one enantiomer in excess takes a chiral influence.
points: Chiral catalysts: Sharpless epoxidation of allylic alcohols, and Noyori asymmetric hydrogenation (Nobel Prize 2001, shared with Knowles).
Chiral auxiliaries, such as Evans' oxazolidinones, are attached to the substrate, direct the reaction and are then removed.
Enzymes, which are chiral catalysts, give very high selectivity.
Enantiomeric excess: ee = (major − minor) ÷ (major + minor) × 100%. A 95:5 mixture is 90% ee.

quiz.q: A reaction gives 95% of one enantiomer and 5% of the other. What is the ee?

entries.name: Ring strain and conformational energy
entries.tagline: Why small rings are reactive and cyclohexane is not.

sections.text: Strain comes from three sources: angle strain (bond angles forced away from 109.5°), torsional strain (eclipsed bonds) and steric strain (atoms crowded close together).
Measured from the heat of combustion per CH₂ compared with an unstrained chain (658.6 kJ/mol per CH₂).
facts: About 115 kJ/mol. The C–C–C angle is 60°, and all bonds are eclipsed.
About 110 kJ/mol. Puckered to reduce eclipsing.
About 0. The chair has ideal angles and all bonds staggered.

points: An axial substituent has unfavorable 1,3-diaxial interactions with the two axial hydrogens on the same side. An equatorial one has none.
The A-value is the energy preference for equatorial over axial. About 7.3 kJ/mol for methyl and above 20 kJ/mol for tert-butyl, which locks the ring in one chair.
In disubstituted rings, the most stable chair has the larger group equatorial. Trans-1,4 can have both equatorial, and cis-1,4 always has one axial.

sections.text: Trans-decalin has two fused chairs and is rigid. Cis-decalin can undergo a ring flip. Steroids have fused rings of this kind.

quiz.q: Why is cyclohexane essentially strain-free?
quiz.a: The chair has ideal bond angles and staggered bonds

entries.name: Alkene reactions: the full toolkit
entries.tagline: Which reagent gives which product, with what regiochemistry and stereochemistry.

facts: Markovnikov. Through a carbocation, so rearrangements are possible. Not stereospecific.
Markovnikov alcohol. No rearrangements, because a mercurinium ion forms. Anti addition.
Anti-Markovnikov alcohol. Syn addition. No rearrangements.
Anti addition through a bromonium ion, giving a vicinal dihalide.
A halohydrin, with OH on the more substituted carbon, anti.
An epoxide. Syn, and the alkene geometry is kept.
OsO₄ (with NMO), or cold dilute KMnO₄
Ozonolysis. The C=C is cleaved into two carbonyl compounds, aldehydes or ketones. With H₂O₂ in the second step, aldehydes become carboxylic acids.
H₂ with Pd, Pt or Ni
Syn addition to give the alkane.
Radical addition, anti-Markovnikov. Only works for HBr.
A cyclopropane, syn, in one step.

sections.text: Br₂ forms a three-membered bromonium ion, and Br⁻ attacks from the opposite face. So cyclohexene gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane, and a Z or E alkene gives a specific diastereomer. Because water, if present as solvent, can also attack the bromonium, a halohydrin forms.

To get the alcohol at the less substituted carbon, use hydroboration–oxidation. To get the more substituted alcohol without rearrangement, use oxymercuration. To break a C=C and find where it was, use ozonolysis.

quiz.q: Which sequence converts a terminal alkene into a primary alcohol?
What does ozonolysis followed by (CH₃)₂S do to an alkene?
quiz.a: Cleaves the C=C into two carbonyl compounds

entries.name: Alkyne chemistry and keto–enol tautomerism
entries.tagline: Triple bonds can be reduced selectively, hydrated to ketones, and extended into longer chains.

sections.text: A terminal alkyne (pKa 25) is deprotonated by sodium amide (NaNH₂) to an acetylide. The acetylide is a good nucleophile and reacts with methyl or primary alkyl halides by SN2 to make a longer alkyne. With secondary or tertiary halides it causes elimination.

facts: Goes all the way to the alkane.
Stops at the cis (Z) alkene, by syn addition.
Gives the trans (E) alkene, by anti addition through a radical anion.

points: H₂O with H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄ adds water in the Markovnikov sense to give an enol, which tautomerizes to a ketone. A terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone.
Hydroboration–oxidation with a bulky borane such as 9-BBN gives the enol of an aldehyde, so a terminal alkyne becomes an aldehyde.

sections.text: An enol and its keto form are constitutional isomers that interconvert by moving a proton, which is tautomerization, and not resonance. The keto form is usually much more stable, because the C=O bond is stronger than C=C. For acetone, the keto form is favored by a factor of about 10⁸. Acid or base catalysis makes the interconversion fast. Enols matter because they are the reactive form in acid-catalyzed α-substitution.

quiz.q: Which reagent reduces an alkyne to a trans alkene?

entries.name: Alcohols, ethers and epoxides: the toolkit
entries.tagline: Turning an OH into a leaving group, oxidizing it carefully, and opening epoxides.

points: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group. Protonation turns it into water (HX, with SN1 for tertiary and SN2 for primary).
Tosylates and mesylates: the alcohol reacts with TsCl or MsCl and pyridine. The C–O bond is not broken, so stereochemistry is retained at the carbon. A later SN2 then inverts it.
SOCl₂ (with pyridine) and PBr₃ convert alcohols to alkyl chlorides and bromides by SN2, with inversion, and avoid carbocation rearrangements.
The Mitsunobu reaction (PPh₃, DEAD and a nucleophile) substitutes an alcohol with inversion in one pot.

facts: Primary alcohol to aldehyde, and secondary to ketone, stopping there because there is no water.
Primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid. Secondary to ketone.

points: Williamson ether synthesis: an alkoxide plus a primary alkyl halide, by SN2. For an unsymmetrical ether, use the less hindered halide.

Epoxides are strained three-membered ethers that open readily. Under basic or nucleophilic conditions the nucleophile attacks the less substituted carbon (SN2). Under acidic conditions it attacks the more substituted carbon, which has more carbocation character. In both cases the attack is from the back, giving trans (anti) products.
Ethers are cleaved by HBr or HI to give alkyl halides.

sections.text: The pinacol rearrangement converts a vicinal diol with acid into a ketone through a carbocation and a shift of an alkyl group. In the Lucas test (ZnCl₂ in concentrated HCl), tertiary alcohols turn cloudy at once, secondary after a few minutes and primary alcohols do not react.

quiz.q: Which reagent oxidizes a primary alcohol to an aldehyde and stops there?
Under basic conditions, where does a nucleophile attack an unsymmetrical epoxide?

entries.name: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls in depth
entries.tagline: Everything a nucleophile can do to a C=O, from acetals to alkenes.

facts: An equilibrium that gives a gem-diol. Formaldehyde is about 99.9% hydrated in water, and acetone only about 0.1%, because ketones are more stable and more hindered.

A hemiacetal first, then an acetal with a second alcohol. Water must be removed to drive it. Acetals are stable to base, Grignard reagents and hydrides, and are removed by aqueous acid. Ethylene glycol is used to protect ketones.
An imine (C=N), with the loss of water. The rate is greatest around pH 4–5. Too acidic and the amine is protonated, too basic and the carbonyl is not activated.
An enamine (C=C–N), which is an enolate equivalent that can be alkylated.
A cyanohydrin. The nitrile can be hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid.

sections.text: A phosphonium ylide (Ph₃P=CHR, made from Ph₃P, an alkyl halide and a strong base) reacts with an aldehyde or ketone to give an alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide. The driving force is the very strong P=O bond.
points: The double bond forms exactly where the carbonyl was, which is its great advantage over elimination.

Unstabilized ylides give mostly Z alkenes. Stabilized ylides (with a C=O next to the carbanion) give mostly E. The Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons variant with phosphonate esters gives E alkenes and the byproduct is water-soluble.
Georg Wittig shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Wolff–Kishner: hydrazine and strong base with heat turns C=O into CH₂. Suitable for acid-sensitive compounds.
Clemmensen: zinc amalgam in HCl does the same, for base-sensitive compounds.
Reductive amination: an aldehyde or ketone with an amine and NaBH₃CN gives an amine, because the iminium is reduced faster than the carbonyl.

quiz.q: Which byproduct drives the Wittig reaction?
quiz.a: Triphenylphosphine oxide, from the strong P=O bond

quiz.q: What protects a ketone during a Grignard reaction elsewhere in the molecule?
wrong: Converting it to an alcohol with NaBH₄

entries.name: Enolates and the aldol family
entries.tagline: Removing the proton next to a carbonyl makes a nucleophilic carbon that builds carbon–carbon bonds.

sections.text: A hydrogen on the carbon next to a carbonyl (the α-hydrogen) is acidic (pKa about 19–20 for ketones, 25 for esters, 9 for 1,3-diketones and 13 for malonate esters) because the enolate is stabilized by resonance. The enolate is nucleophilic at carbon.

facts: LDA (lithium diisopropylamide, pKa of the conjugate acid about 36) at −78 °C in THF. Irreversible and fast. Removes the more accessible, less substituted α-hydrogen.
A weaker base, such as an alkoxide, at higher temperature, so that the enolates equilibrate. Gives the more substituted, more stable enolate.

points: An enolate adds to the carbonyl of another aldehyde or ketone to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound (an aldol).
On heating, or with acid or base, it loses water to give a conjugated enone. The sum is the aldol condensation.
Crossed aldol: if one partner has no α-hydrogens (benzaldehyde, formaldehyde) and the other does, a single product can form. Alternatively, preform the enolate of one partner with LDA.
Intramolecular aldol reactions form five- and six-membered rings readily.

sections.text: An enolate of an ester attacks another ester and expels alkoxide to give a β-keto ester (the Claisen condensation). It needs a full equivalent of base, because the product is acidic (pKa about 11) and its deprotonation is what drives the reaction. The intramolecular version is the Dieckmann condensation, which forms five- and six-membered rings.

A methyl ketone with I₂ and NaOH is halogenated three times at the methyl group and then cleaved, giving a carboxylate and iodoform (CHI₃), a yellow solid. It is a test for methyl ketones (and ethanol).

quiz.q: Which base gives the kinetic enolate of an unsymmetrical ketone?
Why does the Claisen condensation need a full equivalent of base?
quiz.a: Deprotonation of the product drives the reaction

entries.name: Enolate alkylation, Michael and Robinson reactions
entries.tagline: Using enolates to alkylate, to add 1,4, and to build rings.

sections.text: An enolate attacks a primary alkyl halide by SN2. LDA is used to make the enolate completely first, to avoid aldol side reactions. Tertiary halides eliminate instead.

sections.h: Malonic ester and acetoacetic ester syntheses
points: Malonic ester synthesis: diethyl malonate is deprotonated, alkylated once or twice, then hydrolyzed and heated. The β-diacid loses CO₂ (decarboxylation) to give a substituted acetic acid, RCH₂COOH.
Acetoacetic ester synthesis: the same sequence with ethyl acetoacetate gives a methyl ketone, RCH₂COCH₃.
Both rely on a doubly activated, very acidic CH₂ (pKa 9–13), so a mild base such as ethoxide is enough.

sections.text: An α,β-unsaturated carbonyl is electrophilic at the β carbon, as well as at the carbonyl carbon. Soft nucleophiles, such as stabilized enolates, amines, thiols and organocuprates, add 1,4 (conjugate addition) to the β carbon. Hard, strongly basic nucleophiles such as Grignard reagents and organolithiums tend to add 1,2 to the carbonyl.
A Michael addition followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation makes a new six-membered ring containing an enone. It is a standard way to build the ring systems of steroids and terpenes.
An enamine, made from a ketone and a secondary amine such as pyrrolidine, acts as a mild enolate equivalent. It can be alkylated or added to Michael acceptors, and hydrolysis returns the ketone.

quiz.q: What does the malonic ester synthesis give after hydrolysis and decarboxylation?

entries.name: Carboxylic acid derivatives in depth
entries.tagline: Why acyl chlorides are so reactive and amides are not, and what reducing agents do to each.

sections.text: Acyl chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ acid > amide. Reactivity is greatest where the leaving group is the weakest base and where the group shares its electrons least with the carbonyl by resonance. Amides are least reactive, because the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes onto the carbonyl. Nucleophilic acyl substitution goes in two steps through a tetrahedral intermediate: addition, then loss of the leaving group. A derivative can be converted into anything less reactive.

facts: Acid, ester and acyl chloride go to primary alcohols. An amide goes to an amine, since the C=O oxygen is lost.
Ester to aldehyde, stopping because the intermediate is stable at low temperature until the workup.
A tertiary alcohol with two identical R groups. The ketone formed in the middle is more reactive than the ester.
A ketone, with no over-addition, because the tetrahedral intermediate is chelated and stable.
A ketone, because cuprates do not attack ketones.

points: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky: Br₂ and PBr₃ brominate the α-carbon of a carboxylic acid.
β-Keto acids lose CO₂ on gentle heating through a cyclic transition state, giving an enol and then a ketone.
Nitriles are hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids with acid or base and heat, and reduced to primary amines with LiAlH₄.
Amide hydrolysis needs harsh conditions, which is why peptide bonds are stable in water.

quiz.q: Which reagent reduces an ester to an aldehyde?
Which carboxylic acid derivative is the least reactive?

entries.name: Grignard, organolithium and cuprate reagents
entries.tagline: Carbon nucleophiles made from carbon–halogen bonds, and the rules for using them.

points: Grignard: an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium turnings in dry ether or THF, giving RMgX. The magnesium surface is activated with a crystal of iodine or a little dibromoethane. Everything must be anhydrous.
Organolithium: RX with two equivalents of lithium, or by deprotonation or lithium–halogen exchange, for example n-butyllithium.
Gilman reagent: two equivalents of RLi with copper(I) iodide, giving R₂CuLi.

facts: Attack at the less hindered carbon, giving an alcohol two carbons longer.
A carboxylic acid, one carbon longer.

points: The carbon is a very strong base (conjugate acid pKa about 50). Any acidic hydrogen in the same molecule or in the solvent, such as O–H, N–H, S–H, a terminal alkyne or a carboxylic acid, destroys it by protonation. This is why alcohols must be protected before a Grignard step.
Organolithiums are more reactive and more basic than Grignards.
Gilman reagents are softer: they add 1,4 to enones, react with acyl chlorides to give ketones, and do SN2 with alkyl and aryl halides.

sections.text: Air and moisture sensitivity means these reagents are made under nitrogen or argon with dried glassware, as in the techniques of the Schlenk line.

quiz.q: Why can't a Grignard reagent be made in the presence of an alcohol group?
quiz.a: The O–H proton destroys it by protonation

entries.name: Electrophilic aromatic substitution in depth
entries.tagline: The mechanism, why substituents direct where they do, and the limits of Friedel–Crafts.

sections.text: The aromatic ring attacks the electrophile to form a resonance-stabilized carbocation, the arenium ion (sigma complex). That step is slow because aromaticity is lost. A base then removes a proton, restoring the aromatic ring.

points: The substituent decides which arenium ion is more stable. Attack ortho or para to an electron-donating group puts the positive charge next to the substituent, which can stabilize it. Attack meta never does.
Activating, ortho/para directing: –OH, –OR, –NH₂, –NR₂, alkyl groups. Strong activators (OH, NH₂) can react without a catalyst.
Deactivating, meta directing: –NO₂, –CN, –CF₃, –C=O (aldehyde, ketone, acid, ester), –SO₃H.
Halogens are the exception: deactivating, because they withdraw by induction, but ortho/para directing, because their lone pairs stabilize the arenium ion by resonance.
When two groups compete, the stronger activator controls. Steric hindrance favors para over ortho.

facts: The carbocation can rearrange to a more stable one, so propyl chloride gives mostly isopropylbenzene. The product is more reactive than the starting material, so polyalkylation occurs. It fails on strongly deactivated rings.
The acylium ion does not rearrange. The ketone product is deactivated, so only one acyl group adds. A Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner reduction then gives the straight-chain alkylbenzene.

points: Nitration: HNO₃ with H₂SO₄ makes the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺. Reducing the nitro group with H₂/Pd or Sn/HCl gives an aniline.
Sulfonation: fuming H₂SO₄ gives –SO₃H. It is reversible, so the sulfonic acid group can be used as a temporary blocking group.
Halogenation: Br₂ with FeBr₃, or Cl₂ with AlCl₃.

quiz.q: Which Friedel–Crafts reaction avoids carbocation rearrangements?
Which group is a meta director?

entries.name: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution, benzyne and diazonium chemistry
entries.tagline: How to put nucleophiles on a benzene ring, and how an amine becomes almost anything.

points: Needs a leaving group, usually F or Cl, and strong electron-withdrawing groups (such as NO₂) ortho or para to it.
The nucleophile adds to give a resonance-stabilized anion (Meisenheimer complex), then the leaving group leaves.
Addition is the slow step, so the order of leaving groups is F > Cl > Br > I, the reverse of SN2. 2,4-Dinitrofluorobenzene (Sanger's reagent) was used to label the end of a protein.

sections.text: An unactivated aryl halide with a very strong base such as NaNH₂ loses HX to form benzyne, a strained, highly reactive triple bond in the ring. A nucleophile then adds to either carbon, so substituted halides can give mixtures of isomers. Benzyne also undergoes Diels–Alder reactions.
A primary aromatic amine reacts with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0–5 °C to give an aryldiazonium salt, ArN₂⁺. The N₂ is an outstanding leaving group, so the diazonium can be replaced:
facts: Ar–H, replacing the amino group, useful for removing a directing group.
An azo compound Ar–N=N–Ar′, coupling at the para position. The long conjugation makes them colored, and they are the basis of azo dyes such as methyl orange.

sections.text: Diazonium salts are unstable above about 5 °C and can explode when dry, so they are made cold and used immediately in solution.

quiz.q: In SNAr reactions, which leaving group is best?
What does the Sandmeyer reaction do?
quiz.a: Replaces the diazonium group with Cl, Br or CN using copper(I) salts

entries.name: Aromatic heterocycles
entries.tagline: Rings that contain nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur, and why pyridine and pyrrole behave so differently.

facts: A six-membered ring with one N. The nitrogen lone pair lies in the plane of the ring, not in the π system, so it is available for protonation: pKa of the conjugate acid is 5.2. The ring is electron-poor, so electrophilic substitution is slow and goes to C3, while nucleophilic substitution goes to C2 and C4.

A five-membered ring with one NH. The nitrogen lone pair is part of the six-electron aromatic system, so pyrrole is not basic (pKa of the conjugate acid about −3.8). The ring is electron-rich and reacts with electrophiles faster than benzene, at C2.
Like pyrrole, with O or S. One lone pair is in the aromatic sextet. Thiophene is the most aromatic of the three.
Has two nitrogens, one pyrrole-like and one pyridine-like. It is amphoteric. The conjugate acid has pKa about 7, which is why histidine acts as an acid–base catalyst in enzymes.
Fused rings. Indole is in tryptophan. Purines and pyrimidines are the bases of DNA and RNA.

sections.text: Count the electrons. A heteroatom whose lone pair is needed to make the 4n + 2 aromatic sextet (pyrrole N, furan O) holds on to it and is not basic. One whose lone pair is in the plane (pyridine N) is basic.

quiz.q: Why is pyrrole not basic?
quiz.a: The nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic π system
wrong: The lone pair is in an sp orbital

entries.name: Palladium cross-coupling reactions
entries.tagline: Joining two carbon fragments with a palladium catalyst, awarded the 2010 Nobel Prize.

sections.text: Palladium cycles between Pd(0) and Pd(II). In general, Pd(0) inserts into a carbon–halogen bond of an aryl or vinyl halide, a second fragment is delivered to the metal, and the two carbon groups join and leave, regenerating Pd(0).

facts: An aryl or vinyl halide plus an organoboron compound (boronic acid) and a base. Mild, tolerates many functional groups, and boron compounds are stable and low in toxicity. The most widely used.
An aryl or vinyl halide plus an alkene and a base, giving a substituted alkene, usually trans. The alkene inserts into the Pd–C bond and a β-hydride is eliminated.
An aryl halide plus a terminal alkyne, with palladium, copper(I) iodide and an amine base. Makes aryl alkynes.
An organotin compound with a halide. Very tolerant, but tin is toxic.
An organozinc reagent with a halide.
An aryl halide plus an amine, making a C–N bond.

sections.text: They make biaryls and conjugated molecules, for which older methods needed harsh conditions. They are central in making drugs, agrochemicals, polymers and organic electronics. Richard Heck, Ei-ichi Negishi and Akira Suzuki shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The steps of the cycle are explained in the inorganic chemistry section on organometallic catalysis.

quiz.q: Which cross-coupling reaction uses an organoboron compound?

entries.name: Radical reactions in organic synthesis
entries.tagline: Radical stability and selectivity, and why bromination is so much choosier than chlorination.

sections.text: A radical has an unpaired electron. Stability follows the order methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary, and allylic and benzylic radicals are especially stable because of resonance.

points: Chlorination of an alkane is fast and not very selective. The relative rates of tertiary, secondary and primary C–H abstraction are about 5 : 3.8 : 1.
Bromination is slower and much more selective: about 1600 : 82 : 1.

The Hammond postulate explains this. The hydrogen abstraction by Br· is endothermic, so the transition state is late and looks like the radical, so differences in radical stability count a lot. Cl· abstraction is exothermic, with an early transition state.

Allylic and benzylic bromination with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) and light or a radical initiator. NBS supplies a very low concentration of Br₂, so the radical substitution beats addition to the double bond.
Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr with peroxides (ROOR). Br· adds to the alkene first, to give the more stable carbon radical, then the radical abstracts H from HBr. This works only for HBr.
Radical initiators such as AIBN and benzoyl peroxide start polymerization of alkenes.

sections.text: Autoxidation is a radical chain reaction in which oxygen slowly degrades organic materials, from rancid fats to plastics. Antioxidants such as BHT and vitamin E donate a hydrogen atom to the chain-carrying radicals, forming a stable, unreactive radical that stops the chain.

quiz.q: Why is bromination more selective than chlorination?
quiz.a: Its hydrogen abstraction step is endothermic, with a late transition state

quiz.q: What does NBS do?
quiz.a: Supplies a low concentration of Br₂ for allylic bromination

entries.name: Diels–Alder and pericyclic reactions
entries.tagline: Concerted reactions in which electrons move around a ring in one step, governed by orbital symmetry.

sections.text: A conjugated diene and a dienophile (an alkene or alkyne) react in one step to form a cyclohexene (a [4+2] cycloaddition), making two new σ bonds from two π bonds.
points: The diene must be able to adopt the s-cis conformation. Cyclopentadiene is locked s-cis and very reactive. Dienes locked s-trans do not react.

Normal electron demand: an electron-rich diene reacts fastest with an electron-poor dienophile, one with groups such as C=O, CN or NO₂. The reaction is controlled by the HOMO of the diene and the LUMO of the dienophile (frontier molecular orbital theory).
It is stereospecific: a cis dienophile gives a cis product, and a trans one gives trans. Diene substituents that are both outside (E,E) end up cis to each other in the ring.
The endo product is usually favored, with the substituent of the dienophile tucked under the diene, because of favorable secondary orbital interactions.
Example: butadiene and maleic anhydride give a cyclohexene anhydride. Cyclopentadiene dimerizes by Diels–Alder at room temperature, and cracking the dimer by heat regenerates the monomer.
A thermal [4+2] cycloaddition is allowed (6 electrons, 4n + 2). A thermal [2+2] is forbidden, but a photochemical [2+2] is allowed.
Electrocyclic ring closure of a 4n π system is conrotatory when thermal and disrotatory when photochemical. For a 4n + 2 system it is the other way round.

Sigmatropic shifts move a σ bond along a π system. The Cope rearrangement ([3,3]) turns a 1,5-diene into an isomer. The Claisen rearrangement converts an allyl vinyl ether into a γ,δ-unsaturated carbonyl compound, which is driven by forming a strong C=O bond.

sections.text: Otto Diels and Kurt Alder shared the 1950 Nobel Prize. Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui shared the 1981 prize for the orbital-symmetry theory.

quiz.q: What does a Diels–Alder reaction form?
A diene must be in which conformation to react in a Diels–Alder reaction?

entries.name: Rearrangements
entries.tagline: Groups that move to an electron-poor neighbor to give a more stable product.

sections.text: Many rearrangements share one feature: a group migrates, with its bonding electrons, to an adjacent electron-deficient atom.

facts: A 1,2-hydride or alkyl (methyl) shift converts a carbocation into a more stable one. 3-methyl-2-butanol with HBr gives mostly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. A shift can also expand a ring, relieving strain.
A vicinal diol with acid loses water to give a carbocation, then an alkyl shift gives a ketone, with the positive charge ending up stabilized by oxygen.
A ketoxime with acid becomes an amide. The group anti to the leaving group on nitrogen migrates. Cyclohexanone oxime gives caprolactam, the monomer of nylon-6.

A ketone with a peracid (such as mCPBA) is converted to an ester, by insertion of an oxygen. Migratory aptitude: tertiary > cyclohexyl > secondary > phenyl > primary > methyl. The group that migrates keeps its configuration.

A primary amide (with Br₂ and NaOH) or an acyl azide (with heat) rearranges to an isocyanate, which is hydrolyzed to a primary amine with one carbon fewer. The migrating group keeps its configuration.

sections.text: If a product has a different carbon skeleton than expected, look for a carbocation, or an electron-deficient nitrogen or oxygen, next to a group that can shift.

quiz.q: Which product does the Beckmann rearrangement of a ketoxime give?

entries.name: Amine synthesis and reactions
entries.tagline: Ways to make primary, secondary and tertiary amines without ending up with a mixture.

facts: Poor. The product is more nucleophilic than ammonia, so it keeps reacting and gives a mixture.
Potassium phthalimide with a primary alkyl halide (SN2), then hydrazine or base. Makes only primary amines.
Alkyl halide + NaN₃ (SN2), then LiAlH₄ or H₂/Pd. Primary amines, with no over-alkylation.
Aldehyde or ketone + amine + NaBH₃CN. Gives primary, secondary or tertiary amines.
Reduction of nitriles, amides and nitro compounds
LiAlH₄ reduces nitriles and amides. Nitroarenes are reduced to anilines with H₂/Pd or Sn/HCl.
Give primary amines with one carbon fewer.

points: Hofmann elimination: a quaternary ammonium hydroxide is heated and gives the less substituted alkene, the opposite of Zaitsev, because the bulky leaving group makes the base remove the most accessible hydrogen.
Hinsberg test with benzenesulfonyl chloride in base: primary amines give a sulfonamide that dissolves in base, secondary amines give one that does not dissolve, and tertiary amines do not react.

quiz.q: Which synthesis makes only primary amines?
wrong: Reductive amination with a secondary amine

entries.name: Carbohydrate stereochemistry and reactions
entries.tagline: Why glucose is a ring, and how sugars differ at a single carbon.

sections.text: D-Glucose is an aldohexose with four stereocenters. In solution almost all of it is a ring. The OH on C5 attacks the aldehyde at C1 to give a cyclic hemiacetal, a six-membered pyranose ring.

points: The new stereocenter at C1 is the anomeric carbon. The two forms are anomers: α (the C1 OH is trans to the CH₂OH group, axial in the chair) and β (cis, equatorial).
Pure α or β glucose dissolved in water slowly converts through the open-chain form to an equilibrium mixture of about 36% α and 64% β. This change in optical rotation is mutarotation.
β-D-glucopyranose has every substituent equatorial in the chair, so it is the most stable and the most abundant form.

sections.text: Epimers differ at one stereocenter only. Mannose is the C2 epimer of glucose and galactose is the C4 epimer. Five-membered rings are furanoses, such as in fructose and ribose.

points: Glycosides: the anomeric hemiacetal reacts with an alcohol and acid to give an acetal. A glycoside is no longer a reducing sugar, and it does not mutarotate. This is the glycosidic link in disaccharides and polysaccharides.
Reducing sugars have a free hemiacetal that opens to an aldehyde, so they react with Tollens' and Benedict's reagents.
The Kiliani–Fischer synthesis lengthens an aldose chain by one carbon.
NaBH₄ reduces a sugar to an alditol, and mild oxidation gives an aldonic acid.

quiz.q: What do you call two sugars that differ at only one stereocenter?
In β-D-glucopyranose, the substituents on the chair are all…

entries.name: Protecting groups
entries.tagline: Temporarily masking one functional group so that another can be changed.

sections.text: A protecting group blocks a reactive site so it survives a reaction elsewhere, and is then removed cleanly. A good one goes on and comes off in high yield, and is stable to the intervening conditions.

facts: TBSCl and imidazole. Stable to base and many reagents. Removed with fluoride (TBAF) or acid.
Stable to acid and base. Removed by hydrogenolysis (H₂, Pd/C).
From ethylene glycol and acid. Stable to bases, Grignards and hydrides. Removed with aqueous acid.
Added with Boc₂O. Removed by trifluoroacetic acid.
Removed by a base such as piperidine.
Carboxylic acid: methyl, tert-butyl or benzyl ester
Removed by base, acid or hydrogenolysis respectively.

sections.text: Groups that are removed by different, non-interfering conditions are orthogonal, so each can be taken off without disturbing the others. A molecule can carry a Boc, a TBS and a benzyl ether, and each can be removed by acid, fluoride and hydrogen respectively.

Peptides are built one amino acid at a time with the amine and side chains protected. In solid-phase synthesis (Merrifield, Nobel Prize 1984) the growing chain is attached to a resin bead, so excess reagents are simply washed away. Fmoc and Boc strategies are standard.
Each protection and deprotection adds two steps and loses material, so a good synthesis plan tries to avoid them.

quiz.q: What removes a TBS ether?
What is orthogonal protection?
quiz.a: Protecting groups removed by different conditions that do not affect each other
wrong: Using several protecting groups of the same type

entries.name: Retrosynthesis and synthesis strategy
entries.tagline: Planning a synthesis by working backward from the target.

sections.text: In retrosynthetic analysis (developed by E. J. Corey, Nobel Prize 1990), you start with the target molecule and break it into simpler pieces by imagining reactions in reverse. You repeat until you reach cheap, available starting materials. A retrosynthetic arrow is written ⇒.

points: Disconnection: break a bond where a known reaction could make it. Each disconnection gives synthons (idealized fragments), which correspond to real reagents.
Functional group interconversion (FGI): change one functional group into another to make a disconnection possible.
Look at the functional groups. They point to the reactions that could have made the molecule.

facts: Next to the carbon bearing OH: Grignard plus a carbonyl compound.
Wittig, or elimination of an alcohol or halide.
Acyl substitution of an acid derivative.

points: Linear versus convergent: in a linear route the overall yield is the product of the step yields, so 10 steps at 90% give 0.9¹⁰ = 35%. A convergent route builds large fragments separately and joins them late, so fewer steps carry the product through and the overall yield is higher.
Order the steps so that reagents are compatible with the groups present, and protect groups if needed.
Plan stereochemistry early.
Umpolung means reversing the normal polarity of a carbon, such as turning a carbonyl carbon from electrophile to nucleophile with a dithiane.

sections.text: 2-Methyl-2-hexanol is a tertiary alcohol. Disconnecting next to the carbinol carbon gives acetone and a butyl Grignard reagent. Forward: butyl bromide with Mg gives butylmagnesium bromide, which adds to acetone, then H₃O⁺.

quiz.q: A synthesis has 10 steps, each 90% yield, in a straight line. What is the overall yield?
Which disconnection suits a cyclohexene ring?

entries.name: Interpreting NMR, IR and mass spectra
entries.tagline: A step-by-step method for working out a structure from its spectra.

sections.text: Each double bond or ring counts 1, and a triple bond counts 2. Oxygen does not change the count. Benzene rings account for 4.

facts: Next to C=C or C=O (allylic, α)
C–H on carbon bearing O or halogen
1–5, broad and variable. Disappear when D₂O is added.

points: A signal split into n + 1 peaks has n equivalent neighboring hydrogens. The pattern for 1 to 4 neighbors: doublet, triplet, quartet, quintet.
Integration gives the ratio of hydrogens.
Coupling constants J, in Hz: vicinal about 6–8, trans alkene 12–18, cis alkene 6–12, aromatic ortho 7–9 and meta 2–3.
The number of signals is the number of different carbon environments, so symmetry reduces it.
Shifts (ppm): alkyl 0–50, C–O 50–90, alkene and aromatic 100–150, C=O 160–220 (ketones and aldehydes 190–220, acids and esters 160–185).
DEPT-135: CH and CH₃ signals point up, CH₂ down, and quaternary carbons do not appear.

sections.text: COSY shows which hydrogens are coupled. HSQC links each hydrogen to the carbon it is attached to. HMBC shows couplings over two to three bonds, which connects fragments across quaternary carbons and carbonyls.

points: Get the molecular formula (from the high-resolution mass) and work out the DoU.
IR: identify the functional groups, such as C=O at about 1700 cm⁻¹ or O–H at 3300.
Mass spectrum: molecular ion and characteristic fragments.
¹³C: count the environments and spot the carbonyl, aromatic and alkene carbons.
¹H: use integration, shift and splitting to assemble fragments, and check the whole structure against all the data.

sections.text: C₄H₈O₂: DoU = 1. IR shows a strong band at 1740 cm⁻¹ (ester C=O). ¹H NMR: 1.26 ppm (3H, triplet), 2.05 ppm (3H, singlet), 4.12 ppm (2H, quartet). The triplet and quartet are an ethyl group, and the quartet is at 4.1, so it is on oxygen. The singlet at 2.05 is a CH₃ next to C=O. The compound is ethyl acetate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃.

quiz.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of C₆H₆?
In DEPT-135, which carbons point down?

entries.name: Named reactions summary
entries.tagline: A quick reference for the reactions with people's names attached.

facts: Acid + alcohol, acid catalyst → ester + water.
Phosphonium ylide + aldehyde or ketone → alkene.
Enolate + carbonyl → β-hydroxy carbonyl, then enone.
Enolizable carbonyl + aldehyde + amine → β-amino carbonyl.
An aldehyde with no α-hydrogen in concentrated base disproportionates to an alcohol and a carboxylate.
Two aromatic aldehydes with cyanide or a thiamine catalyst → α-hydroxy ketone.
Arene + alkyl or acyl halide, AlCl₃ → alkyl- or acylarene.
Aryl diazonium + CuX → aryl halide or nitrile.
Amide or acyl azide → amine with one carbon fewer.
C=O → CH₂ in base or acid.
Na in liquid NH₃ with an alcohol reduces benzene to 1,4-cyclohexadiene.
Alcohol → inverted ester, azide or other, with PPh₃ and DEAD.
Two carbonyls with low-valent titanium → alkene.

quiz.q: Which reaction turns benzene into 1,4-cyclohexadiene?
